verdict: OK to lend in Hosur two-wheelers, but only to Tier-1/Tier-2 ancillaries and dealers tied to TVS, Ather and Hero programmes, with monthly stock and receivable checks; avoid single-OEM, thin-margin component makers and EV-only startups until the AURIC ramp is visible.
title: Hosur two-wheelers: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
Hosur is an assembly and Tier-1/Tier-2 town: steel, aluminium, plastics and electronics come in, and scooters, motorcycles and EV drivetrains go out to dealers and, increasingly, export ports. **Cash is made on throughput and model mix, not on price** — OEMs set prices and pass commodity swings through with a lag, so a supplier's margin is a spread over conversion cost. Ather's Hosur plant runs near-full at 35,000 units/month against 1.8 lakh Q2 FY27 pre-orders [1], and TVS is adding capacity on the back of a 52% Q2 net jump [2]. **So when a proposal lands, check which OEM programme and which model the borrower's line feeds; if it is a single model, ask what happens to the line in a model changeover.**

## Where value and cash sit
Value sits with the OEM and the tooling owner; the supplier owns the machine and the receivable. **Working capital is the real risk, not capex** — CRISIL notes OEM-dependent suppliers run smaller working capital because of just-in-time procurement and prompt payment, while aftermarket and export sellers carry longer cycles [10]. Ather is putting ₹122 crore into capacity [3], which means tooling and vendor advances flow down. **So structure against the receivable, not the fixed asset: check debtor days by OEM and ask for the purchase order and payment terms in writing; if receivables stretch past the stated OEM cycle, ask why and pull the bank statement.**

## What has changed now
National output is strong — IIP NIC 30 up 25.3% YoY and 22.7% Apr-to-date [D] — and peers confirm it: Bajaj, TVS and Hero all posted strong Q2 with industry sales up 27% [4], and Bajaj calls its EV business margin-accretive domestically [5]. **But Tamil Nadu is the weak spot: state GST collections are down 3.2% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1%, a 9.3 pp gap [D].** Bank credit is running ahead of output by 4.3 pp [D], so some of the growth is leverage, not volume. Hero shows the margin squeeze — share up to 7.3% on scooters and VIDA, but input cost inflation and competitive pressure hit the stock [6][7]. **So treat Hosur demand as real but local cash as tight; if a borrower's GST filings lag the state trend, ask for the reason before sanctioning enhancement.**

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
Pursue Tier-1 and Tier-2 ancillaries with two or more OEM programmes, dealers with TVS/Ather/Hero franchises and demonstrated EV service capability, and logistics or tooling vendors with assigned receivables. **Avoid single-OEM component makers below 12% operating margin, pure EV startups without an OEM order, and aftermarket-only traders carrying long cycles [10].** ICRA flags hedging policy and commodity exposure relative to profits as a core analytical focus [8], so take the hedge book. **Take monthly: stock-and-debtor statements, GST returns, top-three customer receivable ageing, and capacity utilisation; covenant on DSCR and a receivables cap.**

## Early-warning signs
- **Monthly stock statement (monthly):** inventory up while sales flat -> ask for order book and cut limit. - **GST returns (monthly):** filings below the Tamil Nadu trend [D] -> ask for reason and hold enhancement. - **Receivable ageing (monthly):** any OEM beyond stated terms -> ask for the payment advice and reprice. - **Hedge book (quarterly):** unhedged commodity exposure large versus profit [8] -> ask for the hedging policy.
